problem: The answer contradicts Section 2 and itself: it first says a stale block's coinbase pays nothing, then adds that 'any coins that do arrive are locked for 100 blocks'. In Bitcoin a stale block's coinbase output is never part of the longest chain, so no coins 'arrive' to be locked. A student will read this as 'stale coins come but are frozen', which is the opposite of the intended point.
fix: The electricity is already spent, the block is not on the longest chain so its coinbase pays nothing at all, and the 100-block coinbase maturity rule never even comes into play because there is no valid coinbase on the canonical chain.

problem: C is defined only as 'electricity plus hardware cost, in rupees', with no time base, so the subtraction is not consistent with the per-attempt expectation (S + F) × (h ÷ H). Units are stated but the period is not.
fix: Define C as the electricity plus hardware cost incurred over the average time to find one network block, in rupees, so E = (S + F) × (h ÷ H) − C is genuinely expected profit per block attempt.

problem: The threshold is presented as a single number. The original analysis gives about one third; later refinements show it can drop to about one quarter when other miners build on the attacker's block. Stating only 'roughly a third' without the caveat can mislead in a 6-mark answer.
fix: The attacker earns more than its hash share above roughly one third of the network in the original analysis; later work shows the threshold can fall to about one quarter depending on how other miners choose between competing chains. In every case it wastes total network revenue.
